sub: Named after al-muzzammil, “the one wrapped in garments”, in ayah 1
theme: Allah prepares the Prophet ﷺ for the heavy mission ahead: pray at night, recite slowly, rely on Allah and bear the deniers patiently. The last ayah makes the night prayer light for everyone.
story: One of the earliest surahs, revealed in Makkah. Al-muzzammil is a gentle call to the Prophet ﷺ, reportedly after he came home trembling from the first revelation and said, “Wrap me up.” Another report says he wrapped himself in grief when the idolaters called him a magician.

The first part orders long night prayer, as training for the weighty Qur’an and the hard mission ahead. He was already preaching openly, the opposition had grown, and he is told to bear it with patience.

The Prophet ﷺ and his companions prayed most of the night, reportedly for a year, until their feet swelled. Then ayah 20 came, making night prayer light and voluntary. Some date it much later, in Madinah, since it mentions fighting and zakah.

sections.title: Rise at night for a heavy Word
sections.meaning: The Prophet ﷺ is told to rise and pray through the night: half, a little less or a little more, reciting slowly. A heavy Word is coming, the quiet night suits recitation best, and the day is busy. So remember Allah, devote yourself fully to Him and rely on Him alone.
points: O you wrapped up, stand the night except a little
Half, a little less or more; recite with tartīl
We will send down to you a heavy Word
The night is best for recitation; the day is busy
Remember your Lord’s name; devote yourself wholly to Him
Lord of east and west: take Him as your Wakīl
sections.matters: This is how Allah prepared the Prophet ﷺ for revelation and the mission. Before the heavy task comes private training: night prayer, slow recitation, remembrance and complete trust. Strength for the day is built at night.
sections.story: Night prayer was made obligatory here. The Prophet ﷺ and his companions reportedly stood so long, for a year, that their feet swelled. Some could not tell when half the night had passed, so they prayed until morning to be safe.
explained: Yā ayyuhā al-muzzammil: a tender call to the one wrapped in his clothes. Rise and pray at night, not the whole night but half, or a bit less, down to a third, or a bit more, up to two-thirds. Recite with tartīl: slowly, every letter clear, pausing ayah by ayah, so the heart reflects.

Why? A qawl thaqīl is coming: heavy in majesty, heavy to carry out, heavy as it descended. The quiet night brings heart and tongue together, while the day is full of work and moving about. So remember Allah always, devote yourself only to Him, and hand every affair to the Lord of east and west.
teaches: Night prayer builds the strength to carry heavy responsibilities.
Recite slowly and reflect; don’t rush to reach the end of the surah.
Keep some quiet time for Allah once the day’s work is done.
Tawakkul: use the means, then leave the result to Allah.
sections.hook: The first word names the surah, and the next surah opens the same way: yā ayyuhā al-muddaththir. The measure of the night moves half → less → more (3–4).

sections.title: Leave the deniers to Me
sections.meaning: Bear what they say and leave them gracefully. Allah will deal with the comfortable deniers: shackles, fire and choking food, on a Day the mountains turn to sliding sand. A messenger came to them as one came to Pharaoh, who disobeyed and was seized. This is a reminder.
points: Be patient and leave them with grace
Leave Me with the wealthy deniers; give them a little time
Shackles, blazing fire, choking food, painful punishment
Earth and mountains quake; mountains become pouring sand
A messenger to you, as to Pharaoh, who disobeyed and was seized
A Day that turns children grey; the sky splits apart
A reminder: whoever wills takes a path to his Lord
sections.matters: The Prophet ﷺ is not told to hit back but to endure and leave his enemies to Allah. The warning is real: Pharaoh’s end proves it, and the Day is worse. Yet the door stays open: whoever wills can take the path.
sections.story: Ayah 11 was reportedly about the wealthy leaders of Quraysh who mocked him ﷺ; some say those who fed the army at Badr. Reportedly only a short while passed before Badr came.
explained: Ṣabr on what they say, and hajr jamīl: leave them beautifully, without insults or revenge. Allah says: leave Me to deal with the deniers, ulī al-naʿmah, who live in ease. Waiting for them are ankāl, heavy shackles, a blazing fire, food that sticks in the throat and painful punishment, on the Day the mountains collapse into sliding sand.

Makkah is addressed. A messenger was sent to you as a witness, as Mūsā was sent to Pharaoh, and Pharaoh was seized with a crushing grip when he disobeyed. If you disbelieve, how will you shield yourselves from a Day that turns children grey and splits the sky? Allah’s promise comes true. This is a reminder: choose your path.
teaches: Answer insults with patience and dignity, not revenge.
Wealth and comfort protect no one from Allah’s justice.
Pharaoh’s end is a lesson for anyone who rejects a messenger.
Allah gives people a real choice, so choose the path to Him.
sections.hook: The punishments come as a list of four (12–13): shackles, fire, choking food, painful punishment. Rasūl appears three times in 15–16: sent to you, sent to Pharaoh, and the messenger he disobeyed.

sections.title: Allah makes the night prayer light
sections.meaning: Allah knows the Prophet ﷺ and a group with him stood two-thirds, half or a third of the night. They could not keep exact count, so He made it light: recite what is easy. Some will be ill, travelling for a living or fighting. Keep the prayer, give zakah and charity, and seek forgiveness.
points: Your Lord knows you stand two-thirds, half or a third
He knew you couldn’t keep count, so recite what is easy
Some are ill, some travel to earn, some fight
Establish prayer, give zakah, lend Allah a good loan
Good sent ahead waits with Allah, better; seek forgiveness
sections.matters: It shows Allah’s mercy in His law: He knows people’s limits, their illness, work and struggles. The heavy night duty becomes voluntary, while the pillars stay firm: prayer, zakah, charity and seeking forgiveness.
sections.story: After the opening ayat, night prayer was obligatory and feet swelled. Reportedly a year later (some say eight months) this ayah made it light. Others place it about ten years later, in Madinah, because it mentions fighting and zakah.
explained: Your Lord saw your effort: you and a group of believers stood nearly two-thirds of the night, or half, or a third. Allah measures night and day exactly, but you could not. Lan tuḥṣūhu: you couldn’t keep precise count, and some stood all night to be safe. So He turned to you with ease: recite what is easy.

He knows some will be sick, some travelling to earn Allah’s bounty, some fighting in His cause. So pray what is easy, establish the prayer, pay zakah and give a qarḍ ḥasan, a good loan, beyond zakah. Every good sent ahead is found with Allah, better and greater. And seek forgiveness, since every deed falls short.
teaches: Allah never asks more than people can bear.
Night prayer is voluntary now, but pray what is easy for you.
Earning a lawful living is mentioned right beside fighting for Allah.
Your real wealth is what you send ahead.
Seek forgiveness even after doing good.
sections.hook: The whole section is one long ayah, starting with ۞ at the top of page 575. It echoes the opening’s half, less and more as two-thirds, half and a third.

groups.text: O you wrapped up, rise at night: half, a little less or more, and recite the Qur’an slowly.
A heavy Word is coming. The quiet night suits recitation best, while the day is full of work.
Remember Allah, devote yourself wholly to Him, and rely on the Lord of east and west.
Bear their words patiently and leave them gracefully. Leave the wealthy deniers to Allah for a little while.
Shackles, fire, choking food and pain await, on the Day the earth shakes and mountains become sliding sand.
A messenger was sent to Makkah as one was sent to Pharaoh, who disobeyed and was seized severely.
How will deniers escape a Day that turns children grey and splits the sky? His promise comes true.
This is a reminder: whoever wills takes a path to his Lord.
Allah made night prayer light for the sick, travellers and fighters: pray what is easy, give, and seek forgiveness.

1.explain: Yā ayyuhā al-muzzammil: “O you wrapped in your garments.” A gentle, loving way of calling the Prophet ﷺ, to comfort him. Some take it as “O you who were asleep.”
1.why: Reportedly after the first revelation at Ḥirāʾ, when he came home trembling and said, “Wrap me up.” Another report: the idolaters called him a magician who splits friends apart, and he wrapped himself in grief.

2.explain: Qum al-layl: rise and pray at night. Out of mercy, not the whole night, “except a little”. This night prayer was made obligatory at the start.

3.explain: The amount: half the night, or a little less than half, down to about a third.

4.explain: Or a little more, up to about two-thirds. Tartīl: recite slowly and clearly, letter by letter, pausing and reflecting, so the heart is moved.

5.explain: Qawl thaqīl: a heavy Word, the Qur’an. Heavy in majesty, heavy to act on, heavy in the Scales, and heavy as it came: he would sweat on a freezing day.

6.explain: Nāshiʾat al-layl: rising at night to pray. It brings heart, tongue and ears together (or subdues the self more), and recitation is clearer when everything is quiet.

7.explain: Sabḥ ṭawīl: by day you are busy moving about with work, people and duties. So keep the night for worship.

8.explain: Remember your Lord’s name in every way. Tabattal: devote yourself to Him completely and sincerely. This is not monasticism or cutting off family.

9.explain: He is Lord of the east and the west, and there is no god but Him. As you worship Him alone, rely on Him alone: take Him as your wakīl.

10.explain: Be patient with what they say, and hajr jamīl: leave them in a beautiful way, without harm, insults or revenge. This came in Makkah, before fighting was permitted.

11.explain: Dharnī: leave Me to deal with the deniers, ulī al-naʿmah, the people of luxury. Give them a little respite; it won’t last long.
11.why: Reportedly about the wealthy leaders of Quraysh who mocked the Prophet ﷺ; some say those who fed the army at Badr. Reportedly only a short while passed before Badr came.

12.explain: With Us are ankāl, heavy shackles that never open, and jaḥīm, a blazing fire.

13.explain: Ṭaʿāman dhā ghuṣṣah: food that chokes, stuck in the throat, neither going down nor coming up, like zaqqūm. Then a painful punishment beyond what anyone can imagine.

14.explain: On that Day the earth and the mountains shake violently. Solid mountains become kathīb mahīl, a heap of loose sand that slides away.

15.explain: Now Makkah is addressed: We sent you a messenger, Muhammad ﷺ, as a witness to your deeds, just as We sent Mūsā to Pharaoh.

16.explain: Pharaoh disobeyed his messenger, so Allah seized him with akhdh wabīl: a severe, crushing seizure. Beware of the same fate.

17.explain: If you disbelieve, how will you protect yourselves from a Day so terrible it turns children’s hair grey? Either a picture of its horror, or literally so.

18.explain: The sky will split apart from its severity. Kāna waʿduhu mafʿūlā: His promise is always fulfilled; that Day will certainly come.

19.explain: Inna hādhihi tadhkirah: these warnings are a reminder. Whoever wills can take a path to his Lord, through faith and obedience. The choice is real.

20.explain: Night prayer is made light, “what is easy”, because of illness, travel for work and fighting. Keep the prayer and zakah, give charity, and seek forgiveness; every good sent ahead waits with Allah.
20.why: Reportedly the companions prayed long nights for a year until their feet swelled, then this ayah made night prayer light and voluntary. Some say eight months later; others ten years later, in Madinah, since it mentions fighting and zakah.
